title: CRRT circuit monitoring

sources.use: KDIGO 2012: prescribing guideline; summary of Section 5 statements read

manufacturer operator's manual: URL redirects to the Vantive site; not read

objectives: Know the prescription and check that delivered treatment matches it.
Respond to circuit alarms by checking the patient first and using the device's own instructions.
Know when to return blood, stop treatment, document and notify the prescriber.
Explain why the trend in transmembrane pressure and pressure drop matters more than treating an isolated reading as a universal alarm threshold.

items.text: Know the prescription (modality, dose, fluid-balance goal, anticoagulation); report interruptions and under-delivery because KDIGO recommends frequent assessment of delivered dose.
Troubleshoot alarms to minimise downtime and optimise delivered (effluent) dose.
Check the patient first, and review and address the alarm on the screen before clearing it; the alarm off, disable and override buttons decrease alarm sensitivity.
On the device described, the blood pump stops with high-priority (flashing red) alarms; other devices differ.
Confirm the chest radiograph required after internal jugular or subclavian catheter placement has been done and reviewed before first use (KDIGO).

When HIT is clinically likely or confirmed, alert the responsible team immediately and check that the plan addresses every heparin exposure (CRRT anticoagulant, line flushes and catheter locks); do not treat flushes as exempt. A falling platelet count alone does not diagnose HIT; low versus intermediate/high clinical probability determines the heparin-discontinuation pathway, and prescribing decisions follow the treating team.
Who may operate and troubleshoot a CRRT machine is set by competency approval and the unit's policy; the pathway itself says actions are according to local practice guidelines.
Machine, filter set and bag arrangement are device- and software-specific; use the manufacturer's operator's manual for your unit's software version.

Assess the patient first. Report access, return or flow alarms and recent patient or circuit changes to the trained operator. Device-specific tubing, catheter and bag checks must follow the approved local procedure; this lesson does not teach catheter manipulation or alarm clearance.

The transmembrane-pressure (TMP) trend reflects pressure across the filter membrane. A rising trend may indicate membrane fouling or clotting, but flow changes and effluent-line obstruction can also affect it. Interpret the trend with the patient's condition, machine history and local operator guidance; do not diagnose a specific cause from TMP alone.
Priming, set-up, bag changes and alarm-specific actions follow the manufacturer's instructions and the unit's competency programme; the pathway gives device-specific tips only.
Monitor haemodynamics, temperature, fluid balance, electrolytes, acid-base results and bleeding.

At comparable therapy settings, track filter-pressure drop and TMP over time, together with delivered treatment, downtime and catheter function. Do not transfer this centre's machine-specific numerical alarm values to another CRRT device.

During regional citrate anticoagulation, review systemic ionized calcium, the total-to-ionized calcium ratio, calcium supplementation requirements and acid-base trends under the prescribed protocol. Escalate a rising ratio with falling systemic ionized calcium, increasing calcium needs or worsening metabolic acidosis; no single result establishes citrate accumulation.

Escalate persistent alarms to the responsible trained team and prescriber. Blood return or circuit termination must follow the current device instructions and approved local procedure. Do not attempt blood return when circuit safety is uncertain, including suspected clotting, until the trained team has determined the safe response. Record interruptions and any circuit blood loss.
Report bleeding, suspected HIT, access problems, haemodynamic instability and interruptions.
Record delivered dose, interruptions, alarms, the reason for stopping and fluid balance per unit standard.

checklist.text: Confirm the prescription (modality, dose, fluid-balance goal, anticoagulant) before and during treatment.
On any alarm, check the patient first, then the lines, clamps, catheter and bags before clearing it.
Do not use alarm off, disable or override functions to clear an unresolved problem.
Operate and troubleshoot the circuit only as the manufacturer's documentation and your competency approval allow.
Monitor haemodynamics, temperature, fluid balance and bleeding.

For persistent alarms, summon a trained CRRT operator and prescriber. Do not attempt blood return if circuit safety is uncertain, including suspected clotting. Follow the authorised device-specific termination pathway and record any blood loss.
Record delivered dose, interruptions and fluid balance.
Recognise and document unexpected trends in TMP and filter-pressure drop, check the patient and treatment context, and escalate using the unit's device-specific procedure.

During regional citrate anticoagulation, review systemic ionized calcium, the total-to-ionized calcium ratio, calcium supplementation requirements and acid-base trends under the prescribed protocol. Escalate a rising ratio with falling systemic ionized calcium, increasing calcium needs or worsening metabolic acidosis; no single result establishes citrate accumulation.

gaps: The alarm pathway is specific to one device family (PrisMax) and one health service; it is not a cross-manufacturer standard.
The manufacturer's operator's manuals were located but not read: Baxter's Prismaflex 7.xx manual URL now redirects to the Vantive site, and software versions differ by unit.

Priming, citrate and calcium adjustment procedures, numerical thresholds, drug dosing, weaning and device-specific filter-change thresholds are not covered. Selected 2026 Delphi monitoring statements are now mapped; local protocols, lab schedules and independent specialist review are required.
KDIGO 2026 update is a draft; the 2012 guideline is over ten years old.
Full ASH HIT probability-assessment algorithm and locally approved anticoagulant alternatives require clinician and pharmacist review; no stand-alone nursing stop/titrate protocol is taught.
